newsitem.title: USA: Russian central banker worried about budget delay.
newsitem.headline: Russian central banker worried about budget delay.

text.p: The delay of the 1997 budget in the Russian parliament could throw a dark cloud over macroeconomic developments for 1997, said Andrei Kozlov, deputy chairman of the Central Bank of the Russian Federation.
"If by spring there is no clear idea for tax and investment, the year is lost," Kozlov told a Russian Financial Markets seminar on Monday.
The impasse arose not from differences on economic issues but from political disputes over collecting and distributing state resources, Kozlov said.
Since spring and summer are the best seasons to take economic initiatives, progress for the year would be in doubt if the first crucial first three months are squandered in squabbling, he said.
After this year's successful $1 billion global bond debut, Kozlov expected to see more issuance in 1997. The maturity is likely to exceed five years, he added.
But foreign currency bonds meet only part of the need of the Russian government's fiscal deficits, the bulk of which would continue to be financed by the domestic treasury market, Kozlov said.
Funding by the International Monetary Fund, he said, is the "least reliable" because political views often get involved in the decision for disbursement.
Kozlov said the IMF expects Russia to work in certain ways which may not serve Russian interests at a given time.

The declining yields of Russian Treasury bills as a result of moderating inflation and the opening of the GKO market to foreign investors are putting a squeeze on profits of Russian banks, Kozlov said, forecasting 1997 inflation at 11 to 12 percent, down from about 30 percent this year.
Russian banks have about 15 percent of their assets in government securities, whose huge profits have enabled them to offset the losses from problem loans, he said.

Kozlov noted that the dilemma for the central bank is to make the domestic debt market more efficient by reducing yields and bringing more participants to the market and to give banks time to adjust to a new low-inflation environment.
